etymology: From Babylon, the Chaldean empire on the Euphrates, and Latin captivitas, the state of being held as a prisoner of war; the term names the deportation of Judah to Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar.
biblical_def: The Babylonian Captivity was the seventy-year exile of the kingdom of Judah, when Nebuchadnezzar burnt the house of the LORD and carried the people away from their land (2 Kings 25). It was no accident of empire but the righteous judgment of God upon a covenant people who had broken His covenant, despised His prophets, and gone whoring after idols. Jeremiah had foretold both the length and the meaning of it: "And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years" (Jer 25:11). Daniel, reading the prophet, understood the term by the books (Dan 9:2) and turned to confession and supplication. Yet judgment was not the last word. God preserved a remnant in the furnace, kept His promise to David, and brought His people home again, that the Seed might come. The captivity therefore stands as a sober type of the deeper bondage of sin and of the redemption wrought by Christ, who leads captivity captive. This dictionary confesses that God chastens His own in faithfulness, never in caprice, and that even His severest providences serve His covenant of grace.
webster_summary: The seventy-year deportation of Judah to Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar, sent as the righteous judgment of God for covenant-breaking and idolatry. A remnant was preserved and restored, and the captivity stands as a type of bondage to sin and redemption in Christ.
webster_full: BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY, noun. The carrying away of the kingdom of Judah into Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, and their bondage there for seventy years.
It was the judicial sentence of God upon a nation that had filled the cup of its iniquity with idolatry and the shedding of innocent blood.
"And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years" (Jer 25:11).
The captivity required of Judah the just wages of covenant-breaking, yet it preserved a remnant for the promise.
Its sanction is the faithfulness of God, who both chastens and restores His covenant people in mercy.
scriptures: 2 Kings 25:8-9

And in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, which is the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, came Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, unto Jerusalem: And he burnt the house of the LORD, and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great man's house burnt he with fire.
And this whole land shall be a desolation, and an astonishment; and these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years.
Dan 9:2

In the first year of his reign I Daniel understood by books the number of the years, whereof the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet, that he would accomplish seventy years in the desolations of Jerusalem.
2 Chron 36:20
And them that had escaped from the sword carried he away to Babylon; where they were servants to him and his sons until the reign of the kingdom of Persia.
corruption_summary: The chief corruption is to read the exile as mere political misfortune or imperial accident, emptying it of its character as the righteous judgment of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical reconstruction often treats the captivity as a sociological event to be explained by geopolitics alone, and treats the prophets as men reinterpreting disaster after the fact rather than foretelling it by the Spirit. Scripture forbids this. Jeremiah named both the cause and the seventy-year measure before it came to pass, and Daniel read those very words as inspired and dated. To strip the exile of its moral and prophetic meaning is to deny that God governs the nations and chastens His people in covenant faithfulness.

The believer recovers the true principle: God is not mocked, and a people that despises His word and bows to idols will reap what it has sown. Yet the same God who sends the furnace preserves a remnant within it and brings them home in His appointed time. The captivity thus teaches both the severity and the goodness of God, and points beyond itself to the redemption from sin's bondage accomplished in Christ.
roots_summary: The term joins the name of Babylon to the Latin idea of captivity, naming Judah's seventy-year bondage as a covenant sentence.
roots_lines: Babylon — Heb. Babel, the Chaldean city and empire upon the Euphrates, long a biblical figure of pride and confusion.
Captivity — from Latin captivitas, the condition of one taken and held by a conqueror.
The seventy years are fixed by Jeremiah and confirmed by Daniel, a measured, not arbitrary, chastisement.
The deportation came in stages, culminating in the burning of the temple in Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year.
Scripture reads the whole as judgment in righteousness and restoration in mercy, both governed by God.
usage: The Babylonian Captivity was the harvest of generations of idolatry, reaped at last under Nebuchadnezzar.
Daniel counted the years of the Babylonian Captivity from the books of Jeremiah and fell to prayer.
Even in the Babylonian Captivity God kept a remnant, that the promise to David should not fail.

etymology: From Hebrew Yotham, "the LORD is perfect" or "Jehovah is upright," compounded of the divine name and a root meaning whole or complete.
biblical_def: Jotham was the son of Uzziah and the eleventh king of the house of David, reigning in Judah while his father lived out his leprous days apart (2 Kings 15:32-38). The Chronicler renders the verdict that governs his memory: "And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father Uzziah did" (2 Chron 27:2). He built the higher gate of the house of the LORD, fortified the wall of Ophel, and subdued the Ammonites, who brought him tribute. The secret of his strength is named without ambiguity: "So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the LORD his God" (2 Chron 27:6). Yet the record does not flatter him; the high places were not taken away, and the people still sacrificed and burnt incense there. He was a faithful king with an unfinished reformation, and the leaven of compromise he left would work bitterly in his son Ahaz. This dictionary confesses Jotham faithful, as the Chronicler names him, and learns from him that true strength is the fruit of ordering one's ways before God, while it marks the cost of high places left standing.
webster_summary: The faithful son of Uzziah and eleventh Davidic king of Judah, who did right in the sight of the LORD and grew mighty because he prepared his ways before God. Yet the high places remained, an unfinished reform inherited by the wicked Ahaz.
webster_full: JOTHAM, noun. The son of Uzziah and king of Judah, who did that which was right in the sight of the LORD.
He built the higher gate of the temple and the wall of Ophel, and subdued the Ammonites to tribute.
"So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the LORD his God" (2 Chron 27:6).
His reign requires of us the lesson that strength follows the ordering of the heart before God.
Yet the high places left standing were a sanction of judgment passed to his son Ahaz.
scriptures: 2 Kings 15:34
And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD: he did according to all that his father Uzziah had done.
2 Kings 15:35
Howbeit the high places were not removed: the people sacrificed and burned incense still in the high places. He built the higher gate of the house of the LORD.
2 Chron 27:2
And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that his father Uzziah did: howbeit he entered not into the temple of the LORD. And the people did yet corruptly.
2 Chron 27:6
So Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the LORD his God.
corruption_summary: Jotham's account faces no significant modern redefinition; the abiding lesson is the danger of half-reform that leaves the high places standing.
corruption_paragraphs: Jotham is a minor figure in the popular imagination and has attracted no postmodern reinvention. The honest difficulty in his reign is not a cultural distortion but a spiritual one: a genuinely faithful king tolerated the high places, and the people sacrificed there still. Faithfulness in the king did not by itself purge the worship of the land.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that personal uprightness, though commended by God, is no substitute for thorough reformation according to His word. A leader may prepare his own ways before the LORD and yet leave the means of idolatry intact for his children. The strength Jotham gained by preparing his ways before God rebukes every leader who is mighty in works yet slack in tearing down the high places.
roots_summary: Jotham's name binds the divine name to a root of uprightness, fitting for a king the Chronicler names faithful.
roots_lines: Yotham — "the LORD is perfect" or "Jehovah is upright," from the divine name and a root meaning whole or sound.
The name suits a king of whom it is said that he prepared his ways before the LORD his God.
He reigned as regent during Uzziah's leprosy and then in his own right, sixteen years in Jerusalem.
His building works and his Ammonite tribute are marks of strength the Chronicler ties to his godliness.
The unremoved high places stand in the record as the shadow over an otherwise faithful reign.
usage: Jotham grew mighty, the Chronicler says, because he prepared his ways before the LORD his God.
Though Jotham did right, the high places he left standing bore evil fruit in his son Ahaz.
The builders of the higher gate served under Jotham, a faithful king of the house of David.

etymology: From Old English norther and cyningdom, the realm of a king; applied to the ten tribes who broke from the house of David and were called Israel, distinct from Judah in the south.
biblical_def: The Northern Kingdom was the realm of the ten tribes that tore away from the house of David when Jeroboam led the revolt against Rehoboam (1 Kings 12). To secure his throne against the pull of Jerusalem, Jeroboam made two calves of gold and set them in Dan and in Bethel, saying, "behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt" (1 Kings 12:28). This was the original sin of the kingdom, the founding apostasy from which it never repented. From Jeroboam to Hoshea, every king of the north is weighed in the same balance and found wanting: he "walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin" (1 Kings 15:34). Not one was reckoned faithful. The kingdom multiplied prophets and dynasties and blood, but kept the calves, until at last the LORD removed Israel out of His sight and the Assyrian carried them away in 722 BC. This dictionary confesses the Northern Kingdom apostate from its founding, a standing witness that schism rooted in false worship ripens into ruin, and that the LORD will be worshipped in His own way or not at all.
webster_summary: The kingdom of the ten tribes formed by Jeroboam's schism from the house of David, marked from its founding by the golden calves at Dan and Bethel. Every one of its kings walked in the sins of Jeroboam, and it fell to Assyria in 722 BC.
webster_full: NORTHERN KINGDOM, noun. The realm of the ten tribes called Israel, severed from Judah and the house of David under Jeroboam.
Its worship was corrupt from the first, with calves of gold set up at Dan and at Bethel.
"And this thing became a sin: for the people went to worship before the one, even unto Dan" (1 Kings 12:30).
It required of every king the test of Jeroboam, and not one king turned from his sin.
Its sanction was the Assyrian captivity, when the LORD removed Israel out of His sight in 722 BC.
scriptures: 1 Kings 12:28

Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.
1 Kings 12:30
And this thing became a sin: for the people went to worship before the one, even unto Dan.
1 Kings 15:34
And he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and walked in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin.
2 Kings 17:23
Until the LORD removed Israel out of his sight, as he had said by all his servants the prophets. So was Israel carried away out of their own land to Assyria unto this day.
corruption_summary: Jeroboam's golden calves were a counterfeit worship of the true God by forbidden means, the founding corruption that doomed the Northern Kingdom.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeroboam did not openly deny the LORD; he claimed the calves were the very gods that brought Israel up from Egypt. This is the deadly subtlety of will-worship: it keeps the name of God while exchanging His appointed means for the inventions of men, and it makes worship serve the convenience of the throne. The same impulse animates every later corruption that adds to or alters the worship God has commanded.

Scripture answers such corruption with the regulative principle: God is to be worshipped only in the way He has appointed in His word, and not according to imaginations or any other way not prescribed (LBCF 22.1). The Northern Kingdom shows the end of the contrary principle. A schism founded on convenient idolatry could produce reformers and prophets and yet never tear down its calves, and so it ripened into the Assyrian captivity. The lesson stands: false worship, however politically useful, is the seed of national ruin.
roots_summary: The kingdom takes its name from its northward extent and its claim to the name Israel, though its worship was apostate from the schism onward.
roots_lines: Israel — the ten tribes appropriated the patriarch's name, while the throne of David remained with Judah in the south.
The schism under Jeroboam and Rehoboam divided the united kingdom of David and Solomon (1 Kings 12).
The calves at Dan and Bethel were placed at the northern and southern bounds to draw the people from Jerusalem.
Every dynasty — from Jeroboam through Omri, Jehu, and Menahem — retained the calf-worship as state religion.
The end came in 722 BC, when Assyria took Samaria and scattered the ten tribes among the nations.
usage: The Northern Kingdom never repented of the calves Jeroboam set in Dan and Bethel.
Every king of the Northern Kingdom is weighed against Jeroboam and found to have walked in his sin.
When Assyria fell upon the Northern Kingdom in 722 BC, it was the LORD removing Israel out of His sight.

etymology: From Latin reformare, to form again or restore to a former state; applied to the recurring covenant-renewals of the kings of Judah who turned the nation back to the worship of the LORD.
biblical_def: The Reformations of Judah were the recurring seasons of covenant-renewal in which faithful kings of the house of David turned the nation back from idolatry to the worship of the LORD according to His word. Asa took away the altars of strange gods and commanded Judah to seek the LORD God of their fathers (2 Chron 14:3-4). Jehoshaphat sent the law of God through the cities and put away the high places. Hezekiah reopened and cleansed the house of the LORD, broke the brasen serpent that had become an idol, and kept a great passover. The pattern reached its height under Josiah, when the book of the law was found in the temple, read before the king, and made the rule of a sweeping purge: "And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments" (2 Kings 23:3). True reform was never innovation but return; it tore down the high places and recovered the buried word. Yet even Josiah's reform could not finally turn away the wrath kindled by Manasseh. This dictionary confesses that all genuine reformation is a return to the word of God, the very principle the Reformers recovered against the corruptions of Rome.
webster_summary: The recurring covenant-renewals under faithful Davidic kings — Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, and Josiah — who tore down the high places and recovered the book of the law. True reform was always a return to the word, the same principle the Reformation recovered.
webster_full: REFORMATIONS OF JUDAH, noun. The seasons of covenant-renewal in which godly kings turned the nation back to the worship of the LORD.
They were marked by the casting down of high places, the cleansing of the temple, and the keeping of the passover.
"And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments" (2 Kings 23:3).
True reform requires not innovation but return to the word of God already given.
Their sanction and their limit alike teach that no human reform can finally avert judgment apart from the heart God renews.
scriptures: 2 Chron 14:4
And commanded Judah to seek the LORD God of their fathers, and to do the law and the commandment.
2 Kings 18:4

He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan.
2 Kings 22:8
And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.
2 Kings 23:3

And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all their heart and all their soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people stood to the covenant.
corruption_summary: The reformations face no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that true reform is always a return to the word of God, never a fresh human invention.
corruption_paragraphs: The kings who reformed Judah did not devise new worship; they recovered the old, commanded worship that had been buried under generations of compromise. Josiah's reform began the moment the book of the law was found and read. This is the abiding shape of reformation: the church is purified not by progress beyond Scripture but by return to it, casting down the high places that the inventions of men have raised.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that of the Protestant Reformation itself, which was no innovation but a recovery of the gospel and the worship of God from the corruptions of Rome. As Judah's kings tore down the high places and held up the recovered book, so the Reformers held up the open Scripture against will-worship and accumulated tradition. Yet the limit of Josiah's reform — that it could not avert the judgment Manasseh had earned — warns that outward reform must be matched by the heart God alone renews.
roots_summary: The word names a re-forming, a return to a former and better state, here the recovery of the LORD's appointed worship.
roots_lines: Reformare — Latin, to form again, to restore what had been marred to its right shape.
In Judah the re-forming meant tearing down high places and altars of strange gods.
It meant the cleansing and reopening of the temple and the keeping of the appointed feasts.
Above all it meant the recovery of the book of the law and submission of king and people to its words.
The same Latin root names the sixteenth-century Reformation, a return to Scripture against the corruptions of Rome.
usage: The Reformations of Judah were never novelties but returns to the word the nation had forsaken.
Hezekiah's reformation broke even the brasen serpent once Moses had made, for it had become an idol.
Josiah's reformation began the day Shaphan read the recovered book of the law before the king.

pos: noun (proper, one of the twelve tribes)
etymology: From Hebrew Yehudah, "praise" or "praised," the name Leah gave her fourth son saying, "Now will I praise the LORD" (Gen 29:35); the tribe descended from him.
biblical_def: The Tribe of Judah was the fourth son of Jacob by Leah and the tribe that sprang from him, the royal and messianic line of the covenant people. When the dying Jacob blessed his sons, he set Judah above his brethren: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be" (Gen 49:10). To Judah belonged the kingship. From this tribe came David, and the throne God established forever in David's house; from this tribe, after the schism, came the surviving southern kingdom that bore its name. When the ten tribes fell, Judah was preserved, and through it the line ran down to Bethlehem and the manger. The Lamb who was slain is named "the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David" (Rev 5:5), in whom every promise to the tribe is fulfilled. This dictionary confesses that the LORD chose the tribe of Judah not for its worthiness but for His own purpose of grace, that from it should come the Christ, the true King to whom the gathering of the peoples belongs.
webster_summary: The royal and messianic tribe descended from Jacob's fourth son, to whom the scepter was promised. From Judah came David's line and at last the Lion of the tribe of Judah, Christ the King.
webster_full: JUDAH, noun. The fourth son of Jacob and the tribe descended from him, the royal and messianic line of Israel.
To it the kingship was given, and from it the house of David sprang and endured.
"The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come" (Gen 49:10).
Its promise required a King in whom the gathering of the people should be, and pointed beyond David to Christ.
Its glory is sealed in the Lamb, called the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David.
scriptures: And she conceived again, and bare a son: and she said, Now will I praise the LORD: therefore she called his name Judah; and left bearing.
The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.
Micah 5:2

But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.
Rev 5:5
And one of the elders saith unto me, Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof.
corruption_summary: The tribe of Judah faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the unbroken line of the scepter from Judah to Christ, the King of the covenant.
corruption_paragraphs: The promise to Judah is the thread of kingship running through the whole of Scripture, from Jacob's blessing to David's throne to the manger at Bethlehem to the throne of the Lamb. No critical theory has redefined the tribe, but the careless reader may miss the design: God preserved Judah through schism and exile precisely that the scepter should not depart until Shiloh came.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the faithfulness of God to His covenant promise. He chose Judah by sovereign grace, not by merit, and kept the line through every threat — the fall of the north, the captivity of the south, the small remnant returned — until the Lion of the tribe of Judah was born. The believer reads the genealogy of the King as the surety that not one word of God's promise has fallen to the ground.
roots_summary: Judah's name means praise, and the tribe became the seat of the kingship and the cradle of the Christ.
roots_lines: Yehudah — "praise" or "praised," named by Leah in thanksgiving to the LORD (Gen 29:35).
Jacob's blessing gave the scepter to Judah, marking it as the royal tribe (Gen 49:10).
David sprang from Judah, and God established his throne to endure forever.
After the schism the southern kingdom bore the name Judah and was preserved when Israel fell.
The line ran to Bethlehem and to Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Judah and Root of David.
usage: The scepter promised to the tribe of Judah did not depart until Shiloh came.
From the tribe of Judah came David, and from David's line the Christ was born in Bethlehem.
John was told to weep not, for the Lion of the tribe of Judah had prevailed.

etymology: From Hebrew Zekaryah, "the LORD hath remembered," from zakar, to remember, and the divine name; son of Yehoyada, "the LORD knows."
biblical_def: Zechariah the son of Jehoiada was the priest whom the Spirit of God clothed to rebuke Judah for transgressing the commandments of the LORD, and who was murdered at the king's command in the court of the very house of God. His father Jehoiada the priest had preserved the line of David and crowned and counseled king Joash; but when Jehoiada died, Joash hearkened to the princes and forsook the LORD. When Zechariah stood and cried, "Why transgress ye the commandments of the LORD, that ye cannot prosper?" they conspired against him, "and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of the house of the LORD" (2 Chron 24:21). It was the blackest ingratitude, for Joash repaid the kindness of Jehoiada by slaying his son. Dying, the priest said, "The LORD look upon it, and require it" (2 Chron 24:22). Our Lord Himself set this murder at the close of the martyred blood of the old covenant: "the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar" (Matt 23:35). This dictionary confesses Zechariah a faithful martyr, whose blood, like Abel's, cried to God and was required of that generation.
webster_summary: The priest, son of Joash's benefactor Jehoiada, who rebuked Judah for forsaking the LORD and was stoned in the temple court at the king's command. Christ named his blood as the close of the martyred prophets of the old covenant.
webster_full: ZECHARIAH SON OF JEHOIADA, noun. The priest whom the Spirit moved to rebuke Judah, murdered in the temple court by the command of king Joash.
He was the son of Jehoiada, who had preserved David's line and counseled the king, yet was repaid with the blood of his son.
"And when he died, he said, The LORD look upon it, and require it" (2 Chron 24:22).
His witness required of the king repentance, and met instead with murderous ingratitude.
Christ set his blood as the close of the martyred prophets, required of that generation (Matt 23:35).
scriptures: 2 Chron 24:20

And the Spirit of God came upon Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, which stood above the people, and said unto them, Thus saith God, Why transgress ye the commandments of the LORD, that ye cannot prosper? because ye have forsaken the LORD, he hath also forsaken you.
2 Chron 24:21
And they conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of the house of the LORD.
2 Chron 24:22
Thus Joash the king remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but slew his son. And when he died, he said, The LORD look upon it, and require it.
Matt 23:35
That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar.
corruption_summary: Zechariah's martyrdom faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that the faithful witness who reproves sin may be silenced by the powerful, yet his blood is required by God.
corruption_paragraphs: The murder of Zechariah is a study in the hatred of fallen men for the reproof of God's word. The Spirit clothed the priest to call the nation to repentance, and the answer of king and princes was stones. Joash forgot the kindness of the father and slew the son in the very court where God was worshipped, joining ingratitude to murder and sacrilege.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the certainty of divine justice. The dying prayer — "The LORD look upon it, and require it" — was answered within the year, and our Lord wove this very blood into His indictment of the generation that would crucify Him and murder His apostles. The faithful preacher must reckon that the world may stone him for the truth, and that God Himself keeps the account, requiring innocent blood in His own time.
roots_summary: His name confesses that the LORD remembers, and his story proves that the LORD remembers innocent blood to require it.
roots_lines: Zekaryah — "the LORD hath remembered," from zakar, to remember, joined to the divine name.
Yehoyada — "the LORD knows," the faithful priest who crowned and counseled Joash.
The murder occurred in the court of the house of the LORD, an aggravated sacrilege.
His dying cry, "require it," appeals to God as the avenger of innocent blood.
Christ cites his blood as the close of the martyred witnesses of the old covenant (Matt 23:35).
usage: Zechariah son of Jehoiada rebuked Judah for transgressing the commandments of the LORD.
They stoned Zechariah son of Jehoiada in the temple court at the commandment of king Joash.
Our Lord named the blood of Zechariah son of Jehoiada as the close of the martyrs of old.

etymology: From Hebrew Shaphan, "coney" or "rock-badger"; scribe from Latin scriba, a writer or recorder, from scribere, to write.
biblical_def: Shaphan the scribe was the secretary of king Josiah, the man into whose hands Hilkiah the high priest delivered the book of the law found in the house of the LORD. Sent to oversee the repair of the temple, Shaphan received the recovered book, read it himself, and brought it to the king, telling him, "Hilkiah the priest hath delivered me a book. And Shaphan read it before the king" (2 Kings 22:10). When Josiah heard the words of the law, he rent his clothes, and it was Shaphan whom he sent with the company to inquire of the LORD by the prophetess Huldah. Thus a scribe stood at the hinge of Judah's greatest reformation, the faithful servant who handled the word and brought it to the throne. His house proved faithful after him: his son Ahikam stood for the prophet Jeremiah and delivered him from death (Jer 26:24), and his grandson Gedaliah was made governor, while Gemariah, another son, sought to restrain Jehoiakim from burning the prophet's scroll. This dictionary confesses Shaphan a faithful steward of the word of God, and marks how the LORD often raises up a godly household to shelter His truth and His servants in an evil day.
webster_summary: Josiah's scribe, who received the Book of the Law found in the temple, read it before the king, and stood at the center of Judah's great reformation. His faithful house later sheltered the prophet Jeremiah.
webster_full: SHAPHAN, noun. The scribe of king Josiah, who received the book of the law found in the house of the LORD and read it before the king.
He was sent to oversee the temple repairs, and into his hands Hilkiah delivered the recovered book.
"And Shaphan read it before the king" (2 Kings 22:10).
His office required the faithful handling and conveying of the word of God, which he discharged.
His house was blessed, for his sons Ahikam and Gemariah stood for the prophet Jeremiah in evil days.
scriptures: 2 Kings 22:8
And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.
2 Kings 22:10
And Shaphan the scribe shewed the king, saying, Hilkiah the priest hath delivered me a book. And Shaphan read it before the king.
2 Kings 22:13

Go ye, enquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us.
Nevertheless the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, that they should not give him into the hand of the people to put him to death.
corruption_summary: Shaphan's account faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the dignity of faithful service in handling and conveying the word of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Shaphan was no prophet and no king, but a scribe, a recorder and secretary; and yet at the great turning point of Judah's history it was a scribe who carried the recovered word from the priest to the throne. He read it himself, then read it before the king, and Josiah's reformation flowed from that reading. The lesson is the honor God puts upon the faithful handling of His word, even in the quiet office of a clerk.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the kingdom of God is served by faithful stewards of Scripture in every station. Shaphan's godly house outlasted him: Ahikam shielded Jeremiah from death, Gemariah pleaded against the burning of the scroll, and Gedaliah was set as governor over the remnant. The believer learns that quiet faithfulness with the word of God leaves a blessing upon a household for generations.
roots_summary: Shaphan's name is a small creature of the rocks, but his office as scribe set him over the handling of the word of God.
roots_lines: Shaphan — Hebrew for the coney or rock-badger, a small dweller of the crags.
Scribe — from Latin scribere, to write; a recorder, secretary, and officer of state.
He was sent to the temple to number the money and oversee the workmen of the repair.
Into his hands came the book of the law, which he read first himself and then before the king.
His sons Ahikam and Gemariah carried his faithfulness forward, sheltering the prophet Jeremiah.
usage: Hilkiah delivered the book of the law to Shaphan the scribe, who read it before the king.
When Josiah heard Shaphan the scribe read the words of the law, he rent his clothes.
The faithful house of Shaphan the scribe stood for Jeremiah when the princes sought his life.

etymology: From Hebrew Yishmael, "God will hear," from shama, to hear, and El, God; son of Nethaniah, "the LORD hath given."
biblical_def: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah was a man of the royal seed of Judah who, after the fall of Jerusalem, treacherously murdered Gedaliah the governor whom the king of Babylon had set over the poor remnant left in the land. Gedaliah, son of the godly house of Shaphan, had counseled the people to dwell quietly and serve Babylon, that it might be well with them. Warned that Ishmael came to slay him, Gedaliah would not believe it. So "Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and the ten men that were with him, arose, and smote Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan with the sword, and slew him" (Jer 41:2). He slaughtered the Jews and Chaldeans with him, and led away captive the daughters of the king, until Johanan pursued and the people were recovered, though Ishmael himself escaped to the Ammonites. The crime undid the small mercy left to Judah, for the frightened remnant, fearing the wrath of Babylon, fled down into Egypt against the word of the LORD. This dictionary names Ishmael an instrument of treachery whose murder scattered the remnant and drove them into the very land of bondage from which God had once redeemed His people.
webster_summary: A man of the royal seed of Judah who treacherously assassinated Gedaliah, the governor set over the remnant after Jerusalem fell. His murder scattered the survivors and drove the frightened remnant down into Egypt against the LORD's word.
webster_full: ISHMAEL SON OF NETHANIAH, noun. A man of the seed royal of Judah who murdered Gedaliah the governor after the destruction of Jerusalem.
He came under pretense of peace and slew Gedaliah, the Jews, and the Chaldeans who were with him.
"And slew him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land" (Jer 41:2).
His treachery required no provocation, but proceeded from ambition and the seed royal's envy.
Its sanction was the scattering of the remnant, who fled into Egypt for fear of Babylon.
scriptures: 2 Kings 25:25

But it came to pass in the seventh month, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the seed royal, came, and ten men with him, and smote Gedaliah, that he died, and the Jews and the Chaldees that were with him at Mizpah.
Jer 41:2

Then arose Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and the ten men that were with him, and smote Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan with the sword, and slew him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.

Then Ishmael carried away captive all the residue of the people that were in Mizpah, even the king's daughters, and all the people that remained in Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam: and Ishmael the son of Nethaniah carried them away captive, and departed to go over to the Ammonites.
Because of the Chaldeans: for they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had slain Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon made governor in the land.
corruption_summary: Ishmael's treachery faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that envy and ambition, dressed as zeal, destroy the very mercy God has left to a humbled people.
corruption_paragraphs: Ishmael of the seed royal could not bear that a man of Shaphan's house should govern where he reckoned the crown belonged to him, and so he murdered the governor under the cover of a shared meal. His sin compounded murder with betrayal of hospitality and the wholesale slaughter of the helpless. It is the portrait of ambition that will tear down the little good God has spared rather than submit to His ordering of providence.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the bitter fruit of treachery against lawful, God-given order. Gedaliah's rule was the small mercy left to Judah, a place to dwell quietly under chastisement; Ishmael's sword destroyed it, and the terrified remnant fled to Egypt, refusing the prophet's word to stay. So one man's envy undid a nation's last refuge, and the people ran back toward the house of bondage. The believer learns to submit to the hand of God in His providence rather than to grasp by blood what He has not given.
roots_summary: His name says God will hear, yet his deed was treachery; the contrast underscores how a covenant name does not sanctify a wicked heart.
roots_lines: Yishmael — "God will hear," from shama, to hear, joined to El, God.
Nethaniah — "the LORD hath given," the name of his father.
He was of the seed royal, a descendant of the house of David, and envied Gedaliah's rule.
He slew Gedaliah at Mizpah under pretense of peace, with ten men of his company.
His treachery drove the remnant in fear down into Egypt, against the word of the LORD.
usage: Ishmael son of Nethaniah came under pretense of peace and slew Gedaliah the governor.
Of the seed royal, Ishmael son of Nethaniah envied the rule given to Shaphan's grandson.
After Ishmael son of Nethaniah's treachery, the frightened remnant fled into Egypt.

etymology: From Hebrew Abimelek, "my father is king" (or "the king is my father"), from ab, father, and melek, king; an irony in the mouth of one who made himself king by murder.
biblical_def: Abimelech was the son of Gideon by a concubine of Shechem, a man who grasped at a kingship his father had refused and waded to it through the blood of his own house. Persuading the men of Shechem to back him, he hired vain and light fellows, "and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, being threescore and ten persons, upon one stone" (Judg 9:5); only Jotham the youngest escaped, who from mount Gerizim spoke the parable of the bramble king and pronounced a curse. Abimelech reigned three years over Israel by violence, until God sent an evil spirit between him and the men of Shechem, that the cruelty done to Gideon's seventy sons might be requited. So the Scripture renders the verdict plainly: "Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren" (Judg 9:56). As he besieged Thebez, a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon his head and brake his skull; ashamed to die by a woman's hand, he had his armourbearer thrust him through. This dictionary confesses Abimelech a bloody usurper whose tyranny God judged in kind, a standing proof that the LORD repays the wickedness of the proud upon their own heads. (The Philistine kings of Gerar in Genesis 20 and 26 bore the same royal title Abimelech, but are not this man.)
webster_summary: The son of Gideon who murdered his seventy brethren upon one stone and made himself king at Shechem. God repaid his wickedness, and a woman's cast millstone crushed his skull — tyranny judged in kind.
webster_full: ABIMELECH, noun. The son of Gideon who slew his seventy brethren and reigned as a usurper-king over Israel at Shechem.
He hired vain men, murdered the sons of Jerubbaal upon one stone, and ruled three years by violence.
"Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren" (Judg 9:56).
His ambition required innocent blood, and the requiting of that blood was the sanction of his fall.
A woman cast a millstone that brake his skull, and he was thrust through by his own armourbearer.
scriptures: Judg 9:5

And he went unto his father's house at Ophrah, and slew his brethren the sons of Jerubbaal, being threescore and ten persons, upon one stone: notwithstanding yet Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left; for he hid himself.
Judg 9:53
And a certain woman cast a piece of a millstone upon Abimelech's head, and all to brake his skull.
Judg 9:56
Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren.
Judg 9:57
And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads: and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.
corruption_summary: Abimelech's tyranny faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that God renders the wickedness of the proud and the murderer upon his own head.
corruption_paragraphs: Abimelech is the dark counterpart to his father Gideon, who refused the crown saying the LORD should rule over Israel. The son grasped what the father declined, and built his throne on the bodies of his brethren. His brief reign shows the nature of tyranny seized by blood: it can compel for a season, but it cannot escape the justice of God, who governs even the strife between a usurper and his backers.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the moral government of God over the affairs of men. The text states without flinching that God rendered Abimelech's wickedness upon him and brought upon Shechem the curse of Jotham. The millstone that brake his skull was no accident but the appointed wage of murder. The believer reads here that vengeance belongs to the LORD, who will by no means clear the guilty, and that the ambition which sheds innocent blood ripens to its own destruction.
roots_summary: His name claims a royal father, yet he won his crown by murdering his father's house, and God repaid the deed in kind.
roots_lines: Abimelek — "my father is king," from ab, father, and melek, king.
He was Gideon's son by a concubine of Shechem, claiming kinship to press his suit for kingship.
He slew the seventy sons of Jerubbaal upon one stone, sparing none but Jotham who hid.
Jotham's parable of the bramble king pronounced the curse that came upon Abimelech and Shechem.
The Philistine kings of Gerar in Gen 20 and 26 bore the same title, but are distinct from Gideon's son.
usage: Abimelech slew his seventy brethren upon one stone to make himself king at Shechem.
God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech upon his own head, as the Scripture plainly says.
When a woman cast a millstone upon Abimelech's head, the curse of Jotham was fulfilled.

etymology: From Hebrew shophet, a judge, ruler, or deliverer, from shaphat, to judge or govern; rendered judges through Latin judex, one who declares the law.
biblical_def: The Judges were the deliverers whom the LORD raised up to save Israel in the long season between Joshua and the kings, and the book that bears their name records the recurring cycle of their days. That cycle turns through four stations: sin, when Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baalim; servitude, when He sold them into the hand of their enemies; supplication, when in their distress they cried unto the LORD; and salvation, when He raised up a judge to deliver them. So it is written, "Nevertheless the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them" (Judg 2:16). Yet each deliverance proved only a respite, for when the judge was dead the people corrupted themselves more than their fathers (Judg 2:19), and the spiral ran downward through Othniel, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson to the chaos of the closing chapters. The book diagnoses the root of the disorder twice over: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25). This dictionary confesses that the Judges display both the patience of God toward a covenant-breaking people and the misery of men left to their own self-rule, and that they cry out for the true King, the Lord Jesus Christ.
webster_summary: The deliverers God raised up between Joshua and the kings, whose era ran the recurring cycle of sin, servitude, supplication, and salvation. The book closes with Israel in chaos, for there was no king and every man did what was right in his own eyes.
webster_full: THE JUDGES, noun. The deliverers the LORD raised up to save Israel from its oppressors before the days of the kings.
Their age turned in a cycle of sin, servitude, supplication, and salvation, ever spiraling downward.
"Nevertheless the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them" (Judg 2:16).
The cycle required of Israel repentance, and met with the LORD's patient raising up of a deliverer.
Its closing sanction is the verdict that without a king every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
scriptures: Judg 2:16
Nevertheless the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them.
Judg 2:19

And it came to pass, when the judge was dead, that they returned, and corrupted themselves more than their fathers, in following other gods to serve them, and to bow down unto them; they ceased not from their own doings, nor from their stubborn way.
Judg 3:9
And when the children of Israel cried unto the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer to the children of Israel, who delivered them, even Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother.
Judg 21:25
In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
corruption_summary: The age of the Judges faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that self-rule apart from God's King ends in moral chaos, while God's patient deliverances point to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The book of Judges holds up a mirror to fallen human nature: a people who will not keep covenant, who forget their Deliverer as soon as the pressure lifts, and who corrupt themselves more deeply with each turn of the wheel. The deliverers themselves — Gideon, Jephthah, Samson — were flawed and sometimes grievously so, that the glory of every salvation might be seen to belong to the LORD who raised them, and not to the men.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the refrain of the book itself: where there is no king, every man does that which is right in his own eyes, and the end is anarchy and outrage. This is the autonomy of fallen man laid bare, the doing of what seems right to the self in the place of submission to the revealed will of God. The patient deliverances of the era teach the mercy of God, and the closing chaos teaches the need of the true King, whom the LORD has set upon His holy hill, the Lord Jesus Christ.
roots_summary: A judge in Israel was a deliverer and ruler raised by God, not merely one who decides cases at law.
roots_lines: Shophet — Hebrew for a judge, ruler, or deliverer, from shaphat, to judge and govern.
Judge — through Latin judex, one who declares and administers the law.
The judges were charismatic deliverers, raised for a season to break an oppressor's yoke.
The recurring cycle ran sin, servitude, supplication, salvation, then relapse and a deeper fall.
The book's refrain — no king in Israel — frames the era as the misery of self-rule awaiting the true King.
usage: The age of the Judges ran the weary cycle of sin, servitude, supplication, and salvation.
Whenever Israel cried unto the LORD, He raised up one of the Judges to deliver them.
The book of the Judges ends in chaos, for there was no king and every man did right in his own eyes.
